# Storage Classes {.unnumbered}

The four words you may put in front of a declaration: `auto`, `register`, `static`, `extern`.

They control **lifetime** (how long the storage exists) and **linkage** (whether another file can reach the name). They do not change scope — for that see [Scope and lifetime](scope.qmd).

## The table

| Written | Where it is legal | Lifetime | Reachable from another file |
|---|---|---|---|
| *(nothing)*, inside a function | in a block | until the block ends | no |
| *(nothing)*, outside all functions | at file level | whole program | **yes** |
| `auto` | in a block | until the block ends | no |
| `register` | in a block | until the block ends | no |
| `static` | in a block | **whole program** | no |
| `static` | at file level | whole program | **no** |
| `extern` | anywhere | whole program | refers to a definition elsewhere |

Two rows do completely different jobs with the same word — `static` is the one to be careful about.

## static

```c
void counter(void){
    static int calls = 0;    /* created once, survives every return */
    int fresh = 0;           /* new each call                       */
    calls++; fresh++;
}
```

```
calls=1 fresh=1
calls=2 fresh=1
calls=3 fresh=1
```

| `static` on … | does |
|---|---|
| a **local** variable | keeps the value between calls; initialised **once**, not on each call |
| a **file-level** variable or function | hides it from other files |

## extern, and what static at file level prevents

```c
/* a.c */  int shared = 42;          /* the definition */
/* b.c */  extern int shared;        /* "defined elsewhere, trust me" */
```

```
shared from the other file = 42
```

Make it `static int shared = 42;` in `a.c` and the same two files no longer link:

```
Undefined symbols … referenced from …
```

That is the point of file-level `static`: it keeps a name private to one file, so another file cannot reach it even with `extern`.

| | |
|---|---|
| **definition** | reserves the storage — exactly one, in one file |
| **declaration** (`extern`) | promises it exists — may appear in many files |

## register

A **hint** that a variable will be used heavily. Modern compilers decide this for themselves and ignore the hint, so you will rarely write it.

One rule survives and is enforced: **you cannot take the address of a `register` variable.**

```c
register int x = 5;
int *p = &x;        /* error: address of register variable requested */
```

```c
register int x = 5;
x++;                /* fine — x=6 */
```

So `register` cannot be used with anything you need a pointer to, which rules out arrays you intend to pass to a function.

## auto

The default for a variable declared inside a block. Writing it changes nothing:

```c
auto int x = 3;     /* identical to: int x = 3; */
```

You will see it in old code and in textbooks. Do not write it.

::: {.callout-note}
C++ and newer languages reuse `auto` to mean "work out the type for me". In C it has never meant that.
:::

## Globals: when, and the cost

A file-level variable is in scope for every function below it.

| | |
|---|---|
| any function can change it | nothing records which one did |
| two functions can disagree about its state | the bug is in neither of them |
| it makes a function's behaviour depend on invisible input | the signature no longer tells you what it needs |

Prefer passing values in as parameters and returning them out. Use a global when the alternative is genuinely worse — and in this course, that is almost never.

## Choosing

| You want | Use |
|---|---|
| an ordinary variable | nothing — just declare it |
| a value to survive between calls to one function | `static` on the local |
| a helper variable or function private to one file | `static` at file level |
| one variable shared by several files | define it in one file, `extern` it in the others |
| speed | nothing — write clear code and let the compiler optimise |
